1: After Joshua's death the tribes take some territory but leave many Canaanites in place.
Small compromises open the door to bigger ones.
2: A new generation grows up that does not know the Lord. They serve the Baals, fall to enemies, cry out, and God raises judges to save them. Then they fall again.
This pattern of sin, suffering, cry and rescue repeats through the whole book.
3: Othniel defeats a king from Mesopotamia. Left-handed Ehud kills Eglon, the fat king of Moab, with a hidden dagger.
4: The prophetess Deborah judges Israel and sends Barak against Sisera's iron chariots. Sisera flees and is killed by Jael with a tent peg.
Two women carry the day when the men hesitate.
5: A victory song praising God, the tribes who came to fight, and Jael, and rebuking those who stayed home.
One of the oldest poems in the Bible. Victory is turned into praise.
6: Midianite raiders ruin Israel. An angel calls Gideon, the least in his family, a "mighty warrior". He tears down his father's altar to Baal and asks for a sign with a fleece.
God sees what a person can become with his help.
7: God cuts Gideon's army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, so that Israel cannot boast. With trumpets, jars and torches they throw Midian into panic.
God saves through weakness so that the credit is his.
8: Gideon pursues the kings and refuses to be made king: "The Lord will rule over you." But he makes a golden ephod that becomes a snare.
A good leader can end badly.
9: Gideon's son Abimelech murders his seventy brothers and makes himself king. Jotham tells a fable of trees choosing a bramble as king. Abimelech dies when a woman drops a millstone on him.
Power seized by violence destroys itself.
10: After two minor judges, Israel serves many gods and is crushed by Ammon. They cry out, and God says, "Go and cry to the gods you have chosen." They put the idols away.
Real repentance gets rid of the idols.
11: Jephthah, an outcast, defeats Ammon. He had rashly vowed to offer whatever first came out of his house, and it is his only daughter.
A terrible warning against rash vows. God had forbidden human sacrifice.
12: Ephraim quarrels with Jephthah, and civil war follows. Fugitives are identified by how they pronounce "Shibboleth". Three minor judges follow.
Israel is now turning on itself.
13: An angel tells a barren woman she will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from birth. Samson is born.
God prepares a deliverer even when the people have not asked.
14: Samson wants a Philistine wife. He kills a lion with bare hands, later finds honey in its carcass, and poses a riddle at his wedding. His bride betrays the answer.
Samson has great strength and little self-control.
15: Samson burns the Philistines' fields with torches tied to foxes and kills a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone.
God uses even this flawed man against Israel's oppressors.
16: Delilah coaxes out the secret of Samson's strength. His hair is cut, he is blinded and enslaved. At a pagan feast he prays, pushes down the pillars, and dies with his enemies.
Samson's fall comes from playing with temptation. God hears his last prayer.
17: A man named Micah makes a silver idol, sets up a private shrine and hires a wandering Levite as his priest.
"Everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Religion made to order is idolatry.
18: The Danites, looking for land, steal Micah's idol and priest and set up their own shrine in the north.
False worship spreads from one house to a whole tribe.
19: A Levite's concubine is abused all night by men of Gibeah in Benjamin and dies. He sends pieces of her body throughout Israel.
One of the darkest chapters in Scripture. Israel has become like Sodom.
20: The tribes demand justice. Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty, and in the civil war the tribe is nearly wiped out.
Sin left unchecked ends in the people destroying one another.
21: The tribes grieve that one tribe is almost gone and arrange wives for the survivors by violent means.
The book ends: "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."
